utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, April Carter, and Ms. Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is today represented by Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Carter will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Witness Milomir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, would you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Milomir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe for the Court your work background.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1963 in Brekovo, Arilje municipality. I completed my primary school in Ruma and my secondary school in Zemun, Belgrade. I served the Yugoslav People's Army between the 6th of October, 1982 and 1983, in Capljina. Having served my military service I worked in Rumatrans until 1988 when I transferred to department store company as a truck driver. When I left the JNA service, I was assigned to the reserve forces of the JNA, based on my wartime assignment. The situation and the events that transpired in the Socialist Federal Serbian Republic of Yugoslavia happened at the time when I was a truck driver for the department store company, and as soon as I received the summons I reported to my wartime unit in 1991. My service followed there from, on the basis of my wartime assignment, and later on I was transferred to the reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, sir. Speak a little -- slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to highlight specifically, how were you employed in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, in -- or, rather, in earlier January 1992, or in the month of December, I was transferred from the reserve forces of the JNA to the reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia; to be specific, to the police brigade of the MUP of Serbia. However, I remained employed with the department store company in Belgrade. I would merely respond to all the calls from the MUP of Serbia whenever they needed to engage me. In late 1993 and early 1994 I was engaged as a member of the reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia. I was a member of a wartime unit in Gorazde. This part of my service lasted until the 14th of January, 1994, when my unit retreated from Gorazde. Thereafter I was engaged at various check-points around Belgrade, as a member of the Serbian MUP. This took place for fixed period depending on the assignments given by the MUP of Serbia. When necessary I was also used as a driver for the purposes of the MUP of Serbia and of the army of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that your service with the MUP ended on 14 January, 1994. Is it after that time that you became a driver for other activities for the MUP of Serbia and the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You misunderstood what I said. On the 14th of January, 1994, I came back to Belgrade from the field work in Gorazde. I was then hired as a member of the MUP of Serbia, manning check-points around Belgrade, and, when necessary, working as a driver for the purposes of the MUP. Therefore, I continued being a member of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long were you responsible for driving trucks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This happened between January 1994, until the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What took place on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, 1995, to the best of my recollection, it was a Saturday. And I happened to be with my truck in a town called Mrkonjic Grad. The day before I had delivered goods to that town, and on that day, the 4th of August, the goods were unloaded from the truck. I spent the night there. On the morning of the 5th of August, 1995, news reached us of the Croatian army having attacked the Knin Krajina. It was in the course of the afternoon that the first refugees from the Knin Krajina started arriving. Thus, I stayed back in Knin -- or, rather, not in Knin, in Mrkonjic Grad because I was unable to work my way toward Banja Luka and our frontier since all the roads were blocked by the refugees retreating in the direction of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let me be more precise in my question. What stopped you from working after the 4th of August, 1995, in your capacity as a truck driver?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he hasn't said he stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you stop working as a truck driver?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He hasn't said he stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you work as a truck driver?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of the MUP of Serbia, I worked from the 20th of January, 1994, and the last trip I did was on the 4th of August, 1995. I came back to Serbia from that particular trip only in September, due to the border having been closed on account of the in-flow of refugees. So it was only in early September 1995 that I managed to reach Serbia. On my arrival, I returned my uniform and side-arms, and I was assigned to civilian duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to focus on the years of 1994 and 1995. What options did truck drivers have in regards to work during those years?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, I was a member of the reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia. Since I was a professional driver, I was assigned to the duties of driver of trailer trucks. Previously, civilian trucks from civilian companies, be it private or socially owned, had been requisitioned for the purposes of the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now you indicate that civilian trucks from civilian companies had been taken in for the purposes of the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia. Were civilian trucks allowed to be on the road for any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The trucks that were requisitioned for the purposes MUP of Serbia could travel only on the basis of a travel order received from the command of the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia. And while they were officially used for the purposes of either the VJ or the MUP, they could not be otherwise utilized.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What purposes were the VJ and the MUP using trucks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia used trucks to secure supplies for the units in the field, to transport goods for the Republika Srpska and the Serbian Republic of Serbian Krajina to therefore bring in supplies of foodstuffs, fuel, petroleum, ammunition, mines and explosives. The trucks did whatever -- or transported whatever was required by the MUP or the VJ. The driver would simply carry out the task he had been given.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to first focus on the transport of fuel. Were you a part of these types of transportation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How often were you a part of this type of transportation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It so happened that certain -- or, rather, convoys would travel once a week, or twice, depending on the orders received, and on the needs that arose.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. How often were you personally part of this transportation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Most often, every other week a convoy would depart. Depending on the situation, a convoy could also have travelled once a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you indicating that you personally served on these convoys every other week, or, at times, once a week?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes I would travel every week; and sometimes every other week.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that when you were working in this role that you transported whatever was required by the MUP of the VJ and that the driver would simply carry out the task he was given. I'd like to explore a bit with you the process in which you carried out those tasks. How did you first receive such an order or request?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Since I had been assigned to a police brigade, pursuant to the orders of my company commander, I was a part of a company within a brigade, on the basis of the order, my first transport was to be with just a regular trailer truck. I was supposed to go to Kragujevac, to Zastava the special purpose manufacturing company and that I would be given goods to load right there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask the leave of the Court. I'm having difficulty with my knee, and I would ask for the leave of Court. Can I please take this examination from a seated position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You should have mentioned that at the beginning. We would have arranged for that. We're sorry about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I appreciate it very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you had indicated that you were transporting goods. I I'd like to first focus on the fuel that you had mentioned at the -- earlier in your testimony. Can you please describe the process in which you -- you were responsible for transporting fuel?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The first job of work, the first trip of fuel, took place, if I'm not mistaken, in the month of March 1994. I received orders from my superior to report to the Borovica Transport Company, in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: {Previous translation continues]... where I would be assigned a truck that had been requisitioned for the purposes of the MUP of Serbia. As I reached Ruma where the company was --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can just interrupt you for just a moment. You were indicating a place name, specifically that you received orders to report to the Borovic Transport Company. Can you please tell the Court where that was located.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I received orders in my unit and the Borovica Transport Company was in the town of Ruma which is 54 kilometres away from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you began to tell us for a truck that would be requisitioned for the MUP of Serbia. And you ended your statement with, "as I reached Ruma where the company was ..." Can you please move from there and describe the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that my learned friend Ms. Carter has now misstated his testimony. He was speaking about goods that he was transporting; whereas, Ms. Carter now mentioned fuel. He did not get to that point or state anything about fuel. Perhaps the question should be formulated in more precise terms, if we're talking about Borovica Transport Company and Ruma, we should specify how the vehicle belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at page 8, line 8, Madam Carter said: "Sir, you had indicated that you were transporting goods. I would like to first focus on the fuel that you had mentioned at the -- earlier in your testimony. Can you please describe the process in which you were responsible for transporting fuel." So the discussion is around fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you picked up your truck. Then can you please tell what you did from there, when transporting fuel.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I arrived in Ruma, and in the Borovica Transport Company itself, I reported to the individuals that I had been indicated as contact persons by my superiors. I reported to that particular individual on the parking lot outside the company. The individual took me over to the truck that I was supposed to sign for, and I did sign for that particular truck. It was Mercedes 1735, the make, and the fuel tank had the capacity of some 26 to 27.000 litres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, for that detail. Who were you supposed to be transporting -- excuse me, where were you supposed to transport fuel from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I took over the truck, I drove it back to my unit, i.e., the police brigade, which was stationed in what was formerly the JNA barracks on Volgina Street at Zvezdara. In the morning I received orders to take the cistern truck, the tank truck and to take it to the refinery at Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you went back to your unit that was at the JNA barracks. Can you tell us, what country were the JNA barracks located in?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That was formally JNA barracks that had been given to the MUP to use it on Volgina Street at Zvezdara in the town of Belgrade, which was at the time in Federal Serbian Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated that you were transporting the fuel to the Pancevo area. Can you please tell me, where is that located?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not transport --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have a problem in transcript. The witness said in -- on page 10, line 17, he said that the VJ had given the barracks to the MUP for its purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. So-and-so. What's the problem, sir? What is the problem now with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript did not reflect that the barracks had been given to the MUP or deferred to the MUP by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... line 17. It says, sir, that, "that was formally JNA barracks that had been given to the MUP to use it on," and then names of streets are mentioned which couldn't be caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it does not follow from is -- from what is reflected in the transcript, that it was the army that gave the barracks to the MUP. And I felt that that was very important. It is for me. That it was given by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is not clear from that, okay, you have clarified it now. Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Ms. Carter. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you received orders to take the tank truck to the refinery at Pancevo. Can you please tell me where the refinery at Pancevo was located?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Pancevo refinery is roughly 14 to 15 kilometres away from Belgrade. It is situated along the Belgrade-Pancevo-Vrsac road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At any point of time -- for what purpose was the fuel being taken to Pancevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The fuel wasn't being taken to Pancevo. Rather, I went to Pancevo in order to fill up a derivative that I was supposed to do, as ordered, so I went to the refinery at Pancevo for that reason. So I went to Pancevo from Belgrade with an empty tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you were in Pancevo, did you fill that tank?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in Pancevo, and I can't recall exactly when that was, I had to wait for a while, and the order that had already been issued to the refinery in Pancevo, which derivative to pour into the cistern or the tank. When I arrived there, I received the order, the -- a company of the order, and I went to the pump where that derivative was filled up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that for sure. I don't know who issued it, because it had already been there when I arrived. It had been ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just a little confused. We are talking now you filling up a tank in Pancevo. I don't remember, and I may be mistaken, I don't remember hearing what became of the fuel you collected from Borovic Transport Company. Where was that delivered, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that there was a misunderstanding. I picked up an empty truck, fuel truck Borovica in Ruma, and with that truck, empty truck I came to my unit, to the barracks. So there was no fuel in the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And then you go to the barracks. And what happened at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived at the barracks I reported to the duty service of the Serbian MUP that I had returned from my assignment. They told me to park the truck in a designated area, and I handed over the keys to the duty service and went home. In the morning when I got back to work at 6.00, I received the order to go to the Pancevo refinery, where an order was waiting for me as to what was to be loaded or filled in the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'm sorry about that, but I just didn't have that link.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, once you filled your tank in Pancevo, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When the fuel was filled up, when the tank was filled up, and the order for that had already been sent to the refinery office in Pancevo, when I -- on my way to Pancevo, namely, I was told at the unit that once I filled up the truck I should go back to my units in Volga Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What type of order did you receive once you returned to your unit at Volga Street?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to my unit, I parked the truck in a designated area. I went back to -- I went to the duty service with the papers, and handed the papers over. And the duty officer told me that I could go home and that I should report in the morning to my unit, where I will get a further -- further instructions as to what I was to do next.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What were your instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the unit in the morning, and I think it was around 7.00, when I went to work, I considered this to be my work because this was my wartime assignment, my wartime duty, and this was my daily duty that I had to report for. So I went to my unit. I reported. And I was told to wait, pending an order. I went to the cafeteria there, had a cup of coffee. I can't recall exactly what time it was when a police officer came, and told me to report to the duty service, to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once you reported to that duty officer, what type of assignment were you given?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The duty officer told me that the fuel -- the fuel, petroleum products had to be shipped to the territory of Republika Srpska and that the convoy was organised to transport this petroleum product. He told me to prepare a truck, to check how much fuel I had in my own tanks, my truck tanks and to take a travel papers and to await for further instructions. I did that, reported to the duty service again. I said that I had enough fuel in my tanks, that my tank was currently full. He told me to go to the cafeteria and wait for a while and that in about an hour or two I will get further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you receive further instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I received further instructions, to the effect that I was to leave at around 6.00 or 7.00 p.m. and take my truck to Sremska Mitrovica to the Srem Motel which was on the Belgrade-Zagreb highway near Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the motel what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not arrive at hotel Srem. I parked in the parking lot outside the hotel Srem, and there were some other truck there, fuel trucks and also freight trucks and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many trucks were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly what the number of trucks was then, at the time. But as I sit here now, I think there were about 10 to 15 trucks there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were the other trucks MUP as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not all MUP trucks. When I arrived at the parking lot, the trucks were already parked there. There were some trucks that were used that were actually confiscated for the need of the army, that were waiting there. And there were also some trucks from my unit - I think there were three trucks from my unit - two fuel trucks and one freight truck with a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who were responsible for driving these 10 to 15 trucks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say that. I can't tell you who was responsible for those 10 to 15 drivers. We were all in civilian clothes. No one wore any uniform, so I couldn't really tell who was a driver of the Yugoslav army and which driver belonged to the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now you are indicating that -- they didn't wear any uniforms but that they were Yugoslav army or Serbian MUP. Why would you think that those would be the two types of drivers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say with certainty that there were three trucks from my unit, one of them was a freight truck and two fuel trucks. Those were from my unit. Now, in a conversation with -- that I had with the other drivers, I concluded that they were working there for the need of the Yugoslav army, because their vehicles had been requisitioned by the army from various companies, just as the transport vehicle was -- from transport company was requisitioned for the needs of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How were the trucks marked?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The only markings were the standard plates, and there was also a white sheet of paper, a standard letter-sized paper, which had the word "convoy" on it. That was on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were any of the trucks -- could you tell that any of the trucks were MUP or VJ, by looking at them from an outside observer?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't tell that. There was no way of knowing. Besides, I can also say that, as a driver, as a member of the reserve forces of the Serbian MUP, I had papers from travel documents or travel orders from the MUP, and the other drivers had travel orders from the units that they -- the trucks belonged to. So that was the only way to find out, by checking the papers. But just looking at the trucks you couldn't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What happened to those 10 to 15 trucks after the motel?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at the parking lot of the Srem motel in Sremska Mitrovica, the motel on the highway, the other trucks -- some of the other trucks were already there. Maybe one or two trucks arrived after me. There were two transport vehicles of the Yugoslav army, or rather more specifically the MUP army, all terrain vehicles and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request that the witness repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you are requested to repeat the last portion of your answer. The interpreters didn't hear you properly. Could you please repeat yourself. You just said, "There were two transport vehicles of the Yugoslav army, or rather more specifically of the MUP army, all terrain vehicles ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were two all terrain vehicles of the Yugoslav army. They were standard vehicles. They bore the plates of the Yugoslav army. And there were four vehicles of the Serbian MUP, MUP of the Republic of Serbia, bearing their marks. And there were uniformed men sitting in these vehicles, the MUP vehicles. The men who sat in the MUP vehicles were police officers; and in the military vehicles, there were some soldiers. And there were -- if I recall there was an officer and maybe a non-commissioned officer at that point in time, but I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What actually happened to the 10 or 15 trucks that you were with at the Srem hotel, sir? I think that question hasn't been answered here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when we got there, we remained there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the parking lot for about -- we remained there till about 11.00 or 12.00, 11.00 p.m. or 12.00. After that we formed a convoy, a column of trucks. There was an official MUP vehicle driving in front of us; we followed it. And after three or four trucks there would be a military vehicle or a MUP vehicle, so that they escorted us along the highway towards Zagreb. We got off the ramp for Kuzmin and Sid, the exits for Kuzmin and Sid. We drove along the official highway that led to the border crossing from Yugoslavia towards Bosnia, towards Sremska Racma [as interpreted]. So there was a road that went from Kuzmin, Bosa village, and Raca. We drove along this road for some 5 or 6 kilometres, and then we saw a MUP vehicle with the lights flashing. They were on the right-hand side of the road, and there was another vehicle on the left-hand side of the road. The barrier between the two lanes of the highway was removed so that the trucks could take turns there. And there we got off the highway and onto a road that had been built and cut through the forest. I can't remember if that was the Morovica or the Bosut wood. And this road was cut through that wood, and it was gravelled -- gravel was put over it. And we drove down this road, and we were told to shut the lights off. As we were getting off the highway onto this road, I noticed that there was a large iron gate there, which was opened at the moment when we got there. And I noticed two soldiers who were standing near that gate, armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated there were two soldiers. Can you tell me what type of soldier were they, for which government?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: These were soldiers of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also indicated that there was a -- this road was cut through the forest. Are you aware who cut this road?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that with certainty. That road had been cut with a big earth-moving machine, and it was gravelled. But there was also -- at the beginning of this road, there was this huge iron gate, and there was a similar gate at the end of that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for securing this road?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, when we left Sremska Mitrovica up until we got off and onto this road, we were escorted by a military and police patrol. The first vehicle that turned onto this other road was an all terrain vehicle - a VJ vehicle - and it drove through the forest with the lights off.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How far did you drive with the lights off?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell for certain how far this was. This convoy wasn't moving very fast; maybe 30 to 40 kilometres per hour. We kept a distance between the vehicles just in case there was a need to break suddenly. And I would say that this whole trip lasted about 30 to 40 minutes, up until we got onto the bridge reach Raca. That's a bridge crossing over the Sava river.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What occurred once you reached the bridge at Raca?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When we left the village, when we left Sremska Raca, once we cleared the forest we entered this village of Sremska Raca, and then we came to a road. We took a turn for the bridge to the right, and then there was also a railway that we had to cross. This was the Sid-Bijeljina railways. So you had to cross the railway first, and then you would get onto the bridge and cross over the Sava river. The military -- all personnel -- all-terrain vehicles stopped there, and we -- they issued an order to us to cross over the bridge as soon as possible with our lights off.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because we were told that from this bridge to the official border crossing where the police of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - or, rather, the Serbian MUP was, and also a post of the customs services and the police. At this time there were also monitors on border crossings in Yugoslavia, monitors of the European Union, who checked all vehicles leaving the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and going into Serbia and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why were they checking these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Leaving the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia into Bosnia and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Now, I can't say for sure why, but as far as I could hear from what the others were saying, these European Union monitors were probably there pursuant to an agreement between -- an agreement with the Republic of Yugoslavia because at that time the sanctions were in place and certain goods could not be transported from Serbia into Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did the European Union monitors check your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why not. I can't tell you that. We received our orders and acted on them. All these other discussions, they must have been made at a higher level, so I wouldn't know anything about that. But I just know that our vehicle was not checked by the monitors. Whereas I know that earlier, when I drove -- when I shipped some -- for the Prehrana company when I shipped some medication and so on, we were checked, our trucks were checked by the European Union monitors. And when they checked our vehicle they checked the entire vehicle, and then would seal it -- they would place a seal of the European monitors, and such trucks would then legally arrive at the border of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the case of this night-time convoy, what happened once you reached or when you became near these check-points?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no check-points along these roads which we took.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please describe, then, how you crossed into RS territory?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, once we got off the highway and drove through the forest with no lights on, we also crossed the bridge with our lights off. And when we crossed the bridge and into Republika Srpska, we were met there by the police and the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When they met you, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, while we were crossing, they waited for us. There was a vehicle driving in front of us. I can't recall, I think it was a police vehicle. And there was a vehicle of Republika Srpska also. We crossed the border crossing of Republika Srpska where the police of Republika Srpska and the customs officer of Republika Srpska was. There were no controls. We arrived in Dvorovi, that was close to Bijeljina. And they were -- in our vehicles -- we parked our vehicles in the Neskovic company parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: From that company parking lot where did you take the fuel next?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed at this parking lot -- we arrived -- between 2.00 and 3.00 in the morning. There were members of the army of Republika Srpska and the police of Republika Srpska, and we stayed there for about -- till about 6.00 or 7.00 a.m. And then we were -- there we were issued orders as to where the trucks were to go, each separately.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And where did your truck go?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My truck went to Banja Luka, or, rather, to the Kozora barracks of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of where the other trucks went?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: One of my colleagues from the Serbian MUP who also had a fuel -- drove a fuel truck, he drove off to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And where is Brcko located?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Brcko is on the road to Bijeljina; it is about 60 kilometres from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now you indicated that the route that you took through Sremska Raca. Were there any other routes that you took on any other trip?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I went via Sremska Raca on a number of occasions, maybe 5 to 6 times, and I also drove along another road between Mali Zvornik and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What road is this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this road -- we went from Belgrade -- on the highway Belgrade to Zagreb, and then we got off the road at the exit towards Novi Sad and Sabac. And from there to Loznica, Banja Koviljaca, Mali Zvornik. And then we crossed the official border crossing at the Karakaj bridge and drove off towards Mali Zvornik where we got off onto the road that went on to Ljubovija and Bajina Basta, where we then got off into a quarry, that was actually a quarry in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Which country is Mali Zvornik in?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mali Zvornik is in Serbia in the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was the -- the only thing between Mali Zvornik and Zvornik was the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you crossed the Karakaj road, did you use the same techniques in regards to concealing the trucks through turning off lights and that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We did not use the official crossing across the bridge at the -- at Karakaj. We used the only Drina bridge which was closed for traffic, and there were no check-points and no controls there, either by the police of the Republic of Serbia or the police of the Serb -- of Republika Srpska. The trip also took some one to two hours, and the trips were made at night, as with the other route as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of the type of convoy that you're describing, are you aware of anybody else being able to use this bridge, this old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: During the day, the bridge was used by pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the convoys that you participated in, you indicated that you were carrying fuel. Was fuel the only thing that was being transported on those convoys?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What else was being transported?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Such convoys were also used to transport the goods that were not allowed to go across the border. There was a list of goods that were not allowed across the border, which was kept by the European monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What types of goods were not allowed to go across the border?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If the European monitors allowed fuel to be transported, then it would be, and only in cases where it was required for hospitals and such-like. Fuel was not allowed, ammunition, explosives, cement, cigarettes and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that such convoys were also used to transport the goods that were not allowed to go across the border. Are you indicating that the items that were also going across were ammunition, explosives, and that like?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ammunition, explosives, and similar items were also transported.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware where that ammunition and explosives were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can only speak for the instances where I was the driver. I cannot make any assertions where other drivers were involved. I can only talk about the instances where I drove the goods, and that I can speak responsibly about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let's just focus on those. Can you please tell me where you picked up ammunition and explosives?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were instances where I loaded ammunition at the first partisan company in Uzice. There were instances where I loaded automatic rifles and pistols at the specific purpose industry in Zastava in Kragujevac. There would be instances where I would also be loading material and technical equipment for some depots.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where were these locations located? In which country?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They were in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And who -- who was responsible for the locations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't state who was responsible for the locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was not quite clear, as it was formulated, and the witness himself said that he would be speculating. I must admit, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then the witness has told us he can't speculate. Shall we leave it there? You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in regards to the instances where you said -- you indicated you loaded ammunition at the first partisan company. Are you speculating about that, or are you aware that you loaded that ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How could that be speculation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I wasn't certain I understood Mr. Lukic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic said your question was speculative because you asked who was responsible for that location. That's where the objection came.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what type of facility was the first partisan company?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Prvi Partizan is a factory in Uzice which comprised several manufacturing divisions, including an ammunition factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who were they providing ammunition for?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't claim with any certainty who it was they provided ammunition for. I was given orders to go to Prvi Partizan, and my duty was to check what was being loaded onto the truck. I had a specification which clearly stated how many pallets of which type of items were to be loaded. I can't speak about who it was who ordered for the weapons or ammunition to be loaded, where it was that the orders came, that the goods should be loaded for the purposes of Republika Srpska or the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Outside of the goods and the fuel that you transported across the border, were you responsible for transporting anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It may have been the case that 6 to 7 times I would be transporting cigarettes. That was -- that were then taken over by the Centreks company in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let's focus on the transport of April 1994. What type of convoy, if any, were you responsible for in April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have we heard about the transport of April 1994 before?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to narrow him down to that time-period. He was indicating that he was already starting to participate in that type of activity from March 1994 through August of 1995, so I'm trying to focus down to a specific time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what type of work were you doing in April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In April of 1994, ever since I had started working and participating in the convoys, the last convoy I took part was on the 2nd of August, and the goods were unloaded in Mrkonjic Grad on the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But, sir, I think you must listen to the questions. You are being asked about April 1994. Now you're going to August. Can you tell us something about April 1994? And don't tell us about the last one in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, outside of tanker trucks what other type of vehicles did you drive across the border?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're abandoning your other question, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm trying to focus the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Save for tanker trucks, I drove trailer trucks or canvas or tarpaulin-covered trucks. As I said, trailer trucks that had the capacity of 26 tons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, were you ever responsible for driving buses?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was once in March of 1994 that I was given the task from the police brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What task were you given in March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In March 1994, I was given an assignment from my unit to take a bus. We had normally three buses at our disposal within the unit, to take the bus to the VJ barracks in Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why were you taking the buses to the VJ barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I received orders to take the bus to the VJ barracks in Bubanj Potok. As I reached the barracks, I saw that there were several buses there already. It was in the barracks that I received further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And what instructions were those?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The instructions were that the personnel from the Bubanj Potok barracks should be transported to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, specifically to Knin. That was where I drove them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived at the barracks, you indicated that there were three buses at your disposal. How many buses in total were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were six or seven buses in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And the persons that you were set to transport, do you know who they were or what agency or organisation they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The individuals who were supposed to be transported were able-bodied men, who had fled the territories of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, who had failed to respond to the call-ups from the armies of both the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and who had found refuge in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of these person who fled, were anybody else on these buses to be transported to Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you with certainty is that there was this individual with me who I knew earlier on from my civilian life. My wife hails from Backa Topola, and I knew a man called Tomasovic who worked in the VJ barracks in Backa Topola. Since he hailed -- or his origins were in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, I don't know exactly how this came about, but he was assigned to the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, in Knin, and he went along with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my understanding that it is time for the break. If this would be a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed, ma'am. We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, you were indicating that some of the people that were awaiting the buses were individuals who had fled the territories of Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina. Can you please tell me, if you know, how did they come to be at that VJ barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Upon the return from Gorazde, in January of 1994, I was assigned for a while to man the check-point of the MUP of Serbia, which was on the road from Belgrade in the direction of Susin, and its name was Kosa 4. I was assigned to that check-point, and had to carry out assignments given to me, and the others, by the person in charge of that check-point and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how does that -- your work at the check-point relate to the individuals that had fled the RS and RSK who were there at the VJ barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There was a standing order at the check-point, whereby, pursuant to a decree of the Republic of Serbia and the federal state, based on which all the individuals who were not citizens of the FRY and had as their place of residence, a town in Republika Srpska or the Republic the Serbian Krajina, regardless of whether they hold the refugee status or not, if they are able-bodied men, they should be detained on the spot and taken to the nearest police station. Alternatively, duty police patrol could be summoned, which would then take them from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did they find themselves from the nearest police station to the VJ barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They weren't staying at the VJ barracks. Those of us who manned check-points would stop such individuals and inform the police station that had the competence for that particular check-point, for instance, the Kosa 4 check-point had as its competent police station the one that was located in New Belgrade, Novi Belgrade. In our case, therefore, we would be getting in touch with the police officers from the police station at New Belgrade and tell them to come and pick up any such individuals we found.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the VJ barracks, how did those individuals appear? What type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They wore the old uniforms; that's to say, the uniforms of the former JNA; olive-grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What happened to them while they were there at the VJ barracks, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the persons who were detained were -- would first be taken to our seat at Volgina, on Volgina Street, where they would be subjected to medical checks, whereupon they would be transported to Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What occurred at Bubanj Potok?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I was given the assignment to drive a group of these individuals to Knin by bus, by the time I saw them, they were already in uniform and armed. What had happened previously, I don't know. Were they undergoing training or something of the sort, I can't tell you that. My assignment was to take the bus to the barracks, and when I reached the barracks, they were already in uniform and had already -- and had already been issued with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you are indicating while they were on VJ barracks, they were issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I got there, they had already been issued with side-arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of these individuals who were wearing the old JNA uniforms, were there anybody else, any other type of soldier present there at the VJ barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Probably those were regular members of the army of Yugoslavia. I don't know whether among them there were volunteers who wanted to go there of their own volition. I don't know. There were various stories circulated. I can only tell you what I personally saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Taking into account what you personally saw, why do you think that some people were regularly -- regular members of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The individuals who were going to the battlefield were not regular members of the army of Yugoslavia. Rather, from what I gleaned among those present in the VJ barracks who stayed behind in the barracks, were members of the army of Yugoslavia who were assigned there and performed their regular duty there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Once the individuals were loaded onto buses, were there only the members in the old JNA uniforms, or were there anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: These persons wore JNA uniforms. The only thing I can tell you with certainty is that there was this major there who belonged to the army of Yugoslavia, who I knew from before, who hailed from the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I don't know why he was there, whether it was on orders or of his own accord. When I got there with my bus, he told me that he was going to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina for a period of one year.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware what position this man held after that year in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this individual, who I continued socializing with, we were on visiting terms, he rejoined the army of Yugoslavia upon his return. He then went to join the army of Republika Srpska, spent there some while. He was in Trebinje, I believe. Currently, he is a retired colonel of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Moving back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Do we understand you clearly, sir. This man went to the Republic of Serbian Krajina for a year, joined the army there, came back to the VJ, and then went to the Republika Srpska. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when he went to the Republika Srpska, what did he go and do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He served in the VRS garrison in Trebinje. He was with the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please approach the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are being requested to get closer to the microphone when you speak, sir. Thank you, Madam Carter. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Moving back to the buses themselves. What happened once you -- you left the barracks? Who came with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Major Tomasevic, the one I referred to, came along with me. He was seated with me throughout that time, and there were others. We crossed the border in the same manner we did that in the convoy. We went through the wood, across the bridge, into the Republika Srpska, to a place called Dvorovi. There, the buses parted ways. Each went their own way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Starting with the travel between Serbia and Republika Srpska, can you please tell me, how were the buses marked?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The bus I drove had police licence plates. On our arrival in Sremska Mitrovica, these plates were replaced by civilian plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What plate was yours changed to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which particular town the plate was marked with, but it was a civilian plate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And you've indicated that your bus was en route to Knin. How many other, if any, buses went to Knin with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My bus and another bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What -- where did the other buses go?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Some buses left the column near Bijeljina, went to Zvornik. Some went with us, all the way to Banja Luka. So I can't really know for sure. But I know that some buses parted ways in Bijeljina, and some continued with me to Banja Luka. And I also know that, in Prijedor, there was another bus that went another way. And when we arrived there were only two buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived Knin, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I think we are getting absolutely confused here, and I would like both you and counsel to please be specific with your questions and answers. Madam Carter, if you look at page 33, line 9, you started this discussion that we are now on by saying: "Moving back to the buses themselves. What happened once you left the barracks? Who came with you?" He told you that this Major Tomasevic came with him. They went through the wood, crossed the bridge into Republika Srpska. Now -- to a place called Dvorovi. Now, I'm not quite sure, is this en route to Knin, or is Dvorovi the destination at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please describe the route that you took from the VJ barracks to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We left from the barracks in Bubanj Potok, drove on the highway, the Belgrade-Zagreb highway that we had to take through Belgrade across the bridge, across the Sava. Then we went to Ruma and Sremska Mitrovica. At Sremska Mitrovica the convoy was formed, and we continued on the same road towards Zagreb. When we passed the Kuzmin and Sid exit, some 5 or 6 kilometres after that exit where that forest road was, we got off the highway and we drove through the forest. We crossed the bridge in the same way as we did before, without any lights on. We were escorted by the police and the military. We crossed the Sava bridge to the Bosnian side, to be more precise, to Republika Srpska. The border crossing was at Bosanska Raca, that's the name of the place, and then from Bosanska Raca on the way to Bijeljina we went to Dvorovi which was the first bigger town on the way to Bijeljina. After Bijeljina we went towards Brcko via the corridor that had been cut through Semberija. And from there we got on to the road Bosanski Samac-Modrica. I drove to Modrica. At Modrica we crossed the Bosna river. And at a place called Bare, we got on a regional road from Slavonski Brod to Bosanski Brod, towards Doboj and Zenica. And from there we split and went -- drove to Drventa - all the these territories were under the control of Republika Srpska army - and from there we went to Prnjavor and the place called Vlasnica where I took a left turn, went through Trn, Zalozani. And at Banja Luka, we went towards Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Martin Brod, and from there I drove to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, Knin, that is in the Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And you said your bus, as well as some others, went into the RSK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and another bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you had indicated that others had gone to Banja Luka. Can you please tell me, where is Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka is in Bosnia, or to be more precise, in Republika Srpska on the Vrbas river. You can get do Banja Luka if you're travelling through Croatia via Bosanska Gradiska, this is the direct route along the highway, Belgrade-Zagreb. But you could also take the route that was under the control of the Republika Srpska army, where they were in control. And as I explained, that was Drventa, Prnjavor, Klasnice, Banja Luka, those were the places we went through. And from Banja Luka we went to Mrkonjic Grad, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, et cetera, Kotor Varos, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many people were on each bus?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My bus was full. This was a SANOS 415 bus. The capacity was 53 plus 2, meaning 53 people on the bus and the driver and the co-driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were the other buses on this convoy full?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of Vladimir Tomasevic, were there any other individuals that were VJ officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On my bus, as far as I could observe, maybe there was one -- maybe there were one or one non-commissioned officers wearing camouflage uniforms. All the others were wearing the old JNA uniforms. And as far as I could observe, one of those had a staff-sergeant rank. And the other one, I think, was -- had the rank of Warrant Officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were there any other individuals on any other bus that appeared to be commissioned or non-commissioned VJ officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot claim anything. I can't claim that there were officers in other buses. Each driver was responsible for his own bus. The only thing I can claim with certainty is that each bus had as escort either an officer or a non-commissioned officer of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that some of these buses were MUP buses. Who owned the other buses?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: One or two buses had markings of the Yugoslav army; and I think these were TAM buses, TAM 190. And there were 3 or 4 buses from civilian transport companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic, and I will now put some questions to you as Defence counsel as Mr. Perisic, and because you and I speak in the same language, please slow down a bit when you answer the question and make a short break, between my question and your answer so that the interpreters can interpret the entire answer. And I will also try and make a pause between your answer and my question. Mr. Kovacevic, you gave a statement to the OTP representatives in 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Other than this statement of 2003, did you have any other meetings with the OTP representatives where you discussed any of the subjects, relevant subjects other than when you arrived in The Hague now to testify? So did you have occasion to meet with OTP representatives and discuss these issues?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in Belgrade twice; in March 1993 and in April 2003. And after that until I came to The Hague to testify, I did not give any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here, and I suppose that that's what you said also. You said in March 1993, but you probably meant March 2003.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you say he meant March 2003, well, he said March 1993 and April 2003. So is it the correct thing supposed to be March 2003 and April 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversations, or were you interviewed by any other official organs regarding the matters that you discussed with the Prosecutor, the ICTY Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you still a member of the reserve corps of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Since 1999, I'm no longer with the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has your wartime assignment been removed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pause between question and answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, throughout the period, and we will briefly review all those facts that you discussed with the Prosecutor, but, in fact, you discussed with them the facts that you knew about, beginning with the year of 1991 up until 1999, the war in Kosovo. Did you, throughout this period, make any notes for yourself? Did you sort of have any diary or -- of sorts?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did make notes of places I visited, the persons that I met and worked with. I also made some notes about the convoys and the documents and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you use your notes, or did you review them, before you had the interview with the Prosecutor in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did review my notes, and the OTP representatives, in Belgrade, asked that I draw these two sketches of the way the convoys travelled that I described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP Prosecutor ask you to review your notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you still have those notes with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you provided -- when you were interviewed by the OTP representative in March 2003, I assume that your memory or recollection of the events that you were talking about was better then than it is today; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had two interviews with the Prosecutor, on two occasions, two days each.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The first time the -- the first interview lasted two days, and the second one, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the interviewers, the OTP representatives, they did not try in any way to speed up the whole process. They gave you enough time to remember and to tell them about all the events; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were interested in certain topics, and in that sense they put to you questions, specific questions relating to those subjects; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were interested in certain subjects and topics, and they asked me about them, and about the events that I participated in. In some cases they did not go into detail regarding some events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among other things, they wanted to know what you knew about the role of the Yugoslav army in the convoys that you were a part of, the convoys that Ms. Carter asked you about today and to which you testified in 1994 -- about the events in 1994 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the proofing sessions, you had occasion to review your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, during the proofing session with Ms. Carter, you entered certain alterations that relate to several paragraphs, specifically the paragraphs 95, 102, and 103 of your statement. As for the rest, you completely agreed with what you signed in 2003 as a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter in paragraph 102 and 103 said that my statement of 2003 was perhaps such that it would not be quite clear to the Trial Chamber. And she asked me not to go into detail too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you had some minor changes in those paragraphs. But as for the rest, you stand by what you said then, correct, in every other respect?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my questions, I will mainly focus on the topics that we've mentioned today; but, for now, I would like to see, on the screens, your statement, 1D01-0103.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull them up on the screens, specifically pages 2 of the B/C/S, and 2 of the English versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see the bottom of the page so that can I ask the witness to confirm that what is presented here is, indeed, his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature in the left-hand corner, in the bottom left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please just wait for me to put the entire question to you. At paragraph 4, it is stated as follows: "I have been under investigation after a traffic accident. In 1998, I was charged and convicted, but the appeals court overturned the conviction. Other than that, I have never been under investigation. I have never undergone treatment in any mental health institution." My question in relation to the information you provided to the OTP is as follows. Is what you stated here back in 2003 still true today? In the meantime have there been no criminal proceedings or investigations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time my statement was true, but since that period, there was -- there were criminal proceedings instituted against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that up until that period of time there had been no proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had there not been any criminal proceedings against you before 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I only gave a statement in one particular case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel and witness please make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please make a pause between your question and answer, the two of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before 2003, was ever a conviction rendered against you by any court in Serbia or the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was convicted for some deeds, but this dated before 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, what you stated in paragraph 4 was untrue when you stated it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, this was a falsehood that you stated to the OTP representatives at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After 2003 were any final decisions to convict you rendered in respect of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The charge had to do with weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what it meant, what sort of crime was this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Unlawful possession of weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you ever been convicted for fraud?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That was back in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, this had also transpired before the date on which you gave your statement to the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many times were you convicted for fraud?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Only once. There was only one sentence passed against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. But one sentence, but for how many crimes or acts of fraud were you convicted?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Two. But a single sentence was passed against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with economic crime or forgery of official documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was -- this one case where in my own company, I was charged with driving a truckload of goods without adequate documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time -- can you tell us precisely which period of time this was when these unlawful deeds were charged against you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the forgery of documents and the transportation of cement. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Were there any other charges brought against you for fraud before 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, there were none. Not before 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you keep notes of these issues as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have documentation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever reported for fraud to the SUP Zvezdara in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, there was a criminal report citing me, but I provided them with information, and this was never followed up on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Lukic please re-put his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you re-put your question and please break -- take a break in between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologises, Your Honour. I'm doing my best to follow your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- can we have your answer, and please pause, because it is very important for us to have everything reflected in the transcript. I will repeat my question, and you wait a while before answering. Do you recall a criminal report having been filed against you for fraud to the SUP of Cukarica on the 26th of May, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a criminal report filed against me which involved a company --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you begin to answer even before the counsel has finished his question, let alone the interpretation. There are people interpreting at the back there. We want to hear what they are saying, so when you start talking while they're interpreting, we don't hear what they say. Can you, please, just pause a little bit. Can you put the question again, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, my question is this. Do you recall that a criminal report had been filed against you to the SUP of Cukarica on the 24th of May, 1996, for the crime of fraud?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
